Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)aiaaic repository

AIAAIC Repository is a database of incidents and controversies driven by AI, algorithmic and automation systems (MMRS record), "the independent, grassroots public interest collection" of them on its own page, kept by AIAAIC, a grassroots initiative of individuals; its unit is wider than harm (MMRS record).

🗂️ What it is

  • Origin: June 2019, "a private, professional project" on AI's reputational risks, now an open public interest initiative (OECD; MMRS record).2↘
    It started in June 2019 "as a private, professional project to better understand the reputational risks of artificial intelligence" and evolved into an open, public interest initiative that collects, dissects, examines and divulges incidents and issues (OECD catalogue, which the MMRS record quotes and dates it from); EthicAI writes that it was launched as a private initiative in 2019 and is now an open source, public interest initiative.§7 The MMRS record carries the capture at the name as the composition layer's account of the entity, and the Capture Registry (2026-10-29) records that June 2019, 'a private initiative', CC BY-SA 4.0 and 'incidents and controversies' are the OECD catalogue's, where the record took them, a finding checked against the record and the entity's own pages; the catalogue's words are "a private, professional project", and "a private initiative" is EthicAI's.§24
  • Operator: AIAAIC; no person named on its about page; who runs it unchecked (MMRS record).2↘
    It is kept by AIAAIC, which its about page expands as "AI, Algorithmic and Automation Incidents and Controversies" and calls "an independent, politically and technologically non-partisan grassroots public interest initiative" for AI, algorithmic and automation transparency, openness and accountability; the OECD catalogue names aiaaic as its developing organisation, and the MMRS record gives AIAAIC as operator from the repository's page, with the expansion as the repository's other name.§4 Who runs it is, on the about page, "a diverse set of individuals across the world", funded by individuals' donations and taking no funding or in-kind donations from commercial entities; the page names no person, and the MMRS record lists who runs the repository as not yet checked.§5
  • Admits: controversies as controversies, public dispute beside damage; admission does not require harm (MMRS record).1↘
    On the MMRS record's reading its unit is wider than harm: a controversy enters as a controversy, so public dispute about a system is recorded alongside events in which a system caused damage, admission does not require harm, and its name carries three kinds of system, algorithmic and automated as well as AI.§3
  • Users: researchers, journalists, NGOs, policymakers (OECD).1↘
    It is independent of government and industry, and used by researchers, academics, teachers, NGOs (the catalogue writes "NGS"), journalists, policymakers and industry experts (OECD catalogue).§8

🧾 The record

  • Collections: incidents, systems, datasets; highest number AIAAIC2276, an upper bound.1↘
    It holds three collections, incidents, systems and datasets, its entries numbered in one series, the highest listed on 29 October 2026 AIAAIC2276, an upper bound on their count since the list skips numbers (repository page); EthicAI describes entries carrying incident dates, locations, system developers, technologies and harms, searchable and filterable by those attributes.§9
  • Entry: operator, developer, country, sector, purpose, technology, issue, linked sources, a page type.1↘
    One entry page, read for the per-entry fields the MMRS record left unchecked, gives operator, developer, country, sector, purpose, technology and issue ("Operator: Google users", "Developer: Google"), links its system page, the developer's own document and seven news, commentary and analysis sources by URL, glosses hallucination with Wikipedia's definition credited to Wikipedia, and closes with a page type ("Type: Issue") and its published and updated months.§10
  • Taxonomies: ethical issue, external harm, consequence, news trigger, response.1↘
    It classifies by five taxonomies, ethical issue, external harm, consequence, news trigger and response (repository page), which EthicAI describes as a taxonomy of incident types and causes that continues to evolve as more data is collected.§11
  • Intake: anyone may report or improve a page; more open than the OECD monitor (EthicAI).1↘
    Anyone may report an incident or controversy, from the repository page and from every entry ("Report incident 🔥 | Improve page 💁 | Access database 🔢"), and EthicAI sets its intake against the OECD monitor's: "AIAAIC allows more open submissions from a broader set of contributors", where AIM is curated with controlled input; the MMRS record lists intake, fields and count as not yet checked.§12
  • Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (its page; OECD).1↘
    Its content is under CC BY-SA 4.0 by its own page ("AIAAIC content is available to use, copy, adapt, and redistribute under a CC BY-SA 4.0 licence"), and the OECD catalogue gives its usage rights as open source/permissive, Creative Commons and free of charge and its licence as CC BY-SA 4.0 International, which the MMRS record takes from the catalogue.§13

⚖️ Limits

  • Catalogue: the OECD's entries are not vetted or endorsed by the OECD.1↘
    The catalogue's entries are their originating authors' and "are not vetted or endorsed by the OECD or its member countries", and the entry records the tool as a published document whose validity is "Always up to date".§14
  • Trackers: underreporting, verification, coverage gaps (EthicAI).1↘
    EthicAI names the limits of the incident trackers, underreporting, the verification of submitted incidents and coverage gaps, and finds them under the radar outside specialist circles and critical tools in the conversation on AI risk and accountability.§15
  • Record: entry pages, intake and count not read for it; each assertion with source and basis (MMRS record).1↘
    The MMRS record states its own limits and keeps itself apart from the entity: its entry pages, intake process and current count were not read for it, its three sources were read on 2026-10-28 (the repository page for scope and projects, the catalogue for start, scope and licence, the newsletter's about page for its author), the lifecycle is active as observed that day, and each assertion carries a source and a basis.§16

🧭 Neighbours

  • Basin: oldest of three harm repositories, beside the AI Incident Database and the OECD monitor, not merged with either (MMRS record); grassroots where AIM has state backing (EthicAI).2↘
    Against the OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor, EthicAI finds "AIAAIC is grassroots and community-driven" where AIM has formal international backing, and its array wider, "from technical failures to social impacts", where AIM leans to policy-relevant cases, the two "complementary, not competitive".§18 The MMRS record places it as the oldest of the census's three harm repositories, beside the AI Incident Database and the OECD monitor, its typed neighbours, its role harm; the AI Incident Database's record names it a neighbour in the harm basin, marks it by "AIAAIC, controversies, algorithmic and automation", and checks that the AIID is "not merged with the OECD monitor or AIAAIC".§19
  • Newsletter: AIAAIC Alert, weekly, 92 countries; "by Charlie Pownall" in its metadata.1↘
    AIAAIC's weekly Alert newsletter details the latest incidents and controversies and developments in transparency and accountability and is read in 92 countries by its own account (its about page); the page body names no person, its Substack metadata reads "AIAAIC, by Charlie Pownall", and the MMRS record gives Pownall as the newsletter's writer and the repository as the newsletter's subject.§20
  • Glossary: its AI ethics glossary is a venue the archive addresses three terms to (#543).1↘
    The repository's resources include a list of AI and algorithmic repositories, registers and databases and an AI ethics glossary (repository page), and the archive's Hexagonal Lexical Engine (#543, 10 March 2026) names "AI Ethics glossaries (AIAAIC, AI Incident DB)" as the venue for definitions with citations of three of its terms, semantic liquidation, ghost governance and taxonomic violence.§21
  • Wikipedia: the title AIAAIC redirects to a section Ethics of artificial intelligence does not have.1↘
    Wikipedia has no article for it: the title AIAAIC redirects, since 15 September 2025, to a section "AI, Algorithmic, and Automation Incidents and Controversies" of Ethics of artificial intelligence, which the article as fetched on 29 October 2026 does not have, and the article names neither AIAAIC nor its expansion.§23

👁️ On the Overview

  • Indexed: it records Google AI Overviews, glue on pizza (May 2024) to cancer advice (2026).1↘
    Google AI Overviews is among the systems it records, and a 2026 entry (AIAAIC2256) records Google's AI summaries giving cancer patients wrong advice (repository page); the entry of May 2024 records the Overviews telling users to add glue to pizzas, criticised for "factually inaccurate, misleading and nonsensical answers", the glue traced to a troll post and rocks recommended from a satirical Onion article, and Google saying it would refine them by limiting which queries generate summaries.§22
  • Recorded: composition and record share the OECD catalogue and agree; no person named (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).1↘
    Composition and record were built from the same third-party catalogue and agree, neither names who runs the repository, and the composition names no person, not even the newsletter's writer the record names (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).§25

[SYSTEM] The [AIAAIC Repository](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYAHrOzAVGZfmgmPXLQ14E7nF6e0jgTv2WpIKQ3gQvVkoySoLxku58aP_Vg1Nfs-thPwyBW7qhipdpRNxdodRw13LdPlkfh9UOGd7LKICOwLBvNUg3u1LBxMwUSCQiUSa-g) is an independent, open-access public database that tracks real-world incidents, controversies, and harms related to artificial intelligence, algorithms, and automation. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbAHrOzAVGiFj-_MhNCvc6bpj4W8_NQWJvGxeP8FPwByD98S7nMdIykmolKmhsHz02xyCjICqDclb3BdcLC-umCZsS3qI6KxJ7O0Vo0JrER0cVJI2b0VowIgdQycZa3YgzjDycdhtpFeOgbWUNg)]
Key Details

* Launch: Started in June 2019 as a private initiative to monitor transparency and accountability. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESWAHrOzAVjnQUi3UG6xQ_9GQDKjw_CyfPwTL3ENHUNmGc8BAGkDsQaiW5sLSL1hZ7EU4EgBZcN9F-ZfOYw5Ay3xg78Cv5ZuWN_bmjiwjT_FqTo81iTUsE0sU), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbAHrOzAVGiFj-_MhNCvc6bpj4W8_NQWJvGxeP8FPwByD98S7nMdIykmolKmhsHz02xyCjICqDclb3BdcLC-umCZsS3qI6KxJ7O0Vo0JrER0cVJI2b0VowIgdQycZa3YgzjDycdhtpFeOgbWUNg)]
* Scope: Covers algorithmic discrimination, autonomous vehicle crashes, deepfakes, privacy breaches, workplace automation accidents, generative AI copyright violations, and chatbot hallucinations. * Audience: Used globally by researchers, journalists, civil society groups, and policymakers. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESbAHrOzAVGiFj-_MhNCvc6bpj4W8_NQWJvGxeP8FPwByD98S7nMdIykmolKmhsHz02xyCjICqDclb3BdcLC-umCZsS3qI6KxJ7O0Vo0JrER0cVJI2b0VowIgdQycZa3YgzjDycdhtpFeOgbWUNg)]

Expansion · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)25 sentences · every one sourced below

The AIAAIC Repository

The AIAAIC Repository is a database of incidents and controversies driven by AI, algorithmic and automation systems (MMRS record), its unit the incident or controversy involving such a system (MMRS record), and on its own page "The independent, grassroots public interest collection of incidents and ethical controversies caused by and associated with AI, algorithms, and automation." The OECD's catalogue entry (uploaded 8 June 2023) describes "an independent, open, public interest resource" detailing incidents and controversies, its card on the Overview's rail reading "independent, open-access", the repository's own card lists its incidents as AI and algorithmic automation harms from autonomous vehicle crashes to generative AI copyright and training, and EthicAI (24 April 2025) gives its goal as "systematically documenting incidents where AI systems cause or contribute to harms", a collective memory for the AI field; the MMRS record quotes the catalogue's description and takes the repository's self-description from it. On the MMRS record's reading its unit is wider than harm: a controversy enters as a controversy, so public dispute about a system is recorded alongside events in which a system caused damage, admission does not require harm, and its name carries three kinds of system, algorithmic and automated as well as AI.

It is kept by AIAAIC, which its about page expands as "AI, Algorithmic and Automation Incidents and Controversies" and calls "an independent, politically and technologically non-partisan grassroots public interest initiative" for AI, algorithmic and automation transparency, openness and accountability; the OECD catalogue names aiaaic as its developing organisation, and the MMRS record gives AIAAIC as operator from the repository's page, with the expansion as the repository's other name. Who runs it is, on the about page, "a diverse set of individuals across the world", funded by individuals' donations and taking no funding or in-kind donations from commercial entities; the page names no person, and the MMRS record lists who runs the repository as not yet checked. Its mission is "to make AI, algorithmic and automation systems transparent, open and accountable", by data for academic and civil society entities, by education and by making the case to policymakers and businesses, on the belief that everyone should know when such a system is used on them (about page). It started in June 2019 "as a private, professional project to better understand the reputational risks of artificial intelligence" and evolved into an open, public interest initiative that collects, dissects, examines and divulges incidents and issues (OECD catalogue, which the MMRS record quotes and dates it from); EthicAI writes that it was launched as a private initiative in 2019 and is now an open source, public interest initiative. It is independent of government and industry, and used by researchers, academics, teachers, NGOs (the catalogue writes "NGS"), journalists, policymakers and industry experts (OECD catalogue).

It holds three collections, incidents, systems and datasets, its entries numbered in one series, the highest listed on 29 October 2026 AIAAIC2276, an upper bound on their count since the list skips numbers (repository page); EthicAI describes entries carrying incident dates, locations, system developers, technologies and harms, searchable and filterable by those attributes. One entry page, read for the per-entry fields the MMRS record left unchecked, gives operator, developer, country, sector, purpose, technology and issue ("Operator: Google users", "Developer: Google"), links its system page, the developer's own document and seven news, commentary and analysis sources by URL, glosses hallucination with Wikipedia's definition credited to Wikipedia, and closes with a page type ("Type: Issue") and its published and updated months. It classifies by five taxonomies, ethical issue, external harm, consequence, news trigger and response (repository page), which EthicAI describes as a taxonomy of incident types and causes that continues to evolve as more data is collected.

Anyone may report an incident or controversy, from the repository page and from every entry ("Report incident 🔥 | Improve page 💁 | Access database 🔢"), and EthicAI sets its intake against the OECD monitor's: "AIAAIC allows more open submissions from a broader set of contributors", where AIM is curated with controlled input; the MMRS record lists intake, fields and count as not yet checked.

Its content is under CC BY-SA 4.0 by its own page ("AIAAIC content is available to use, copy, adapt, and redistribute under a CC BY-SA 4.0 licence"), and the OECD catalogue gives its usage rights as open source/permissive, Creative Commons and free of charge and its licence as CC BY-SA 4.0 International, which the MMRS record takes from the catalogue.

The catalogue's entries are their originating authors' and "are not vetted or endorsed by the OECD or its member countries", and the entry records the tool as a published document whose validity is "Always up to date". EthicAI names the limits of the incident trackers, underreporting, the verification of submitted incidents and coverage gaps, and finds them under the radar outside specialist circles and critical tools in the conversation on AI risk and accountability. The MMRS record states its own limits and keeps itself apart from the entity: its entry pages, intake process and current count were not read for it, its three sources were read on 2026-10-28 (the repository page for scope and projects, the catalogue for start, scope and licence, the newsletter's about page for its author), the lifecycle is active as observed that day, and each assertion carries a source and a basis.

The OECD tags it "incident database" and types it a risk management framework, an awareness-building and an education and training tool, the MMRS record's kind is database, and EthicAI defines the AI incident such trackers hold as "any situation where an AI system causes, contributes to, or is associated with an outcome that negatively impacts individuals, groups, systems, or the environment". Against the OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor, EthicAI finds "AIAAIC is grassroots and community-driven" where AIM has formal international backing, and its array wider, "from technical failures to social impacts", where AIM leans to policy-relevant cases, the two "complementary, not competitive". The MMRS record places it as the oldest of the census's three harm repositories, beside the AI Incident Database and the OECD monitor, its typed neighbours, its role harm; the AI Incident Database's record names it a neighbour in the harm basin, marks it by "AIAAIC, controversies, algorithmic and automation", and checks that the AIID is "not merged with the OECD monitor or AIAAIC".

AIAAIC's weekly Alert newsletter details the latest incidents and controversies and developments in transparency and accountability and is read in 92 countries by its own account (its about page); the page body names no person, its Substack metadata reads "AIAAIC, by Charlie Pownall", and the MMRS record gives Pownall as the newsletter's writer and the repository as the newsletter's subject.

The repository's resources include a list of AI and algorithmic repositories, registers and databases and an AI ethics glossary (repository page), and the archive's Hexagonal Lexical Engine (#543, 10 March 2026) names "AI Ethics glossaries (AIAAIC, AI Incident DB)" as the venue for definitions with citations of three of its terms, semantic liquidation, ghost governance and taxonomic violence.

Google AI Overviews is among the systems it records, and a 2026 entry (AIAAIC2256) records Google's AI summaries giving cancer patients wrong advice (repository page); the entry of May 2024 records the Overviews telling users to add glue to pizzas, criticised for "factually inaccurate, misleading and nonsensical answers", the glue traced to a troll post and rocks recommended from a satirical Onion article, and Google saying it would refine them by limiting which queries generate summaries.

Wikipedia has no article for it: the title AIAAIC redirects, since 15 September 2025, to a section "AI, Algorithmic, and Automation Incidents and Controversies" of Ethics of artificial intelligence, which the article as fetched on 29 October 2026 does not have, and the article names neither AIAAIC nor its expansion.

The MMRS record carries the capture at the name as the composition layer's account of the entity, and the Capture Registry (2026-10-29) records that June 2019, 'a private initiative', CC BY-SA 4.0 and 'incidents and controversies' are the OECD catalogue's, where the record took them, a finding checked against the record and the entity's own pages; the catalogue's words are "a private, professional project", and "a private initiative" is EthicAI's. Composition and record were built from the same third-party catalogue and agree, neither names who runs the repository, and the composition names no person, not even the newsletter's writer the record names (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)aiaaic repository

AIAAIC Repository is "the independent, grassroots public interest collection of incidents and ethical controversies caused by and associated with AI, algorithms, and automation" (its own page), kept by AIAAIC.

🗂️ What it is

  • Origin: June 2019, a private, professional project on AI's reputational risks (OECD; EthicAI).1↘
    It began in June 2019 as a private, professional project to understand the reputational risks of AI and became an open, public interest initiative (OECD); EthicAI calls it a private initiative of 2019, now open source.§2
  • Operator: a grassroots initiative of individuals, donor-funded (about page).1↘
    Its maker is AIAAIC, "AI, Algorithmic and Automation Incidents and Controversies", a non-partisan grassroots initiative for transparency, openness and accountability, a diverse set of individuals funded by individuals' donations, with no commercial funding (about page), and the developing organisation in the OECD's catalogue.§3
  • Licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (its page; OECD).1↘
    Its content is CC BY-SA 4.0 (its page; the OECD, free of charge, open source/permissive), and the catalogue calls the entry always up to date.§8

🧾 The record

  • Entries: incidents, systems, datasets, to AIAAIC2276; five taxonomies; per-entry operator, developer, issue, sources.2↘
    It holds incidents, systems and datasets, entries numbered to AIAAIC2276 on 29 October 2026, classified by five taxonomies and carrying dates, locations, developers, technologies and harms searchable by attribute (repository page; EthicAI).§5 An entry gives operator, developer, country, sector, purpose, technology and issue, links its sources and a Wikipedia gloss, and carries a page type, as the May 2024 entry on Google AI Overviews telling users to add glue to pizzas shows, typed "Issue"; AIAAIC2256 records Google's AI summaries giving cancer patients wrong advice.§6
  • Intake: anyone may report or improve a page.1↘
    Anyone may report an incident or improve a page (repository and entry pages), and EthicAI finds its submissions more open and its array wider than the OECD monitor's, the AIAAIC grassroots and the two complementary.§7

⚖️ Limits

  • Trackers: underreporting, verification, coverage gaps (EthicAI); the OECD does not vet its catalogue.1↘
    The OECD tags it an incident database and types it a risk-management, awareness and education tool, not vetted by the OECD; EthicAI defines the AI incident broadly and names the trackers' limits, underreporting, verification and coverage gaps, calling them under the radar but critical.§9

Expansion · The field's ontology — L_F(B)10 sentences · every one sourced below

The AIAAIC Repository

On its own page the AIAAIC Repository is "the independent, grassroots public interest collection of incidents and ethical controversies caused by and associated with AI, algorithms, and automation"; the OECD catalogue (8 June 2023) describes an independent, open public interest resource detailing incidents and controversies, its card reading "open-access", and EthicAI (24 April 2025) a collective memory documenting incidents where AI systems cause or contribute to harms, the repository's card listing its incidents as harms. It began in June 2019 as a private, professional project to understand the reputational risks of AI and became an open, public interest initiative (OECD); EthicAI calls it a private initiative of 2019, now open source.

Its maker is AIAAIC, "AI, Algorithmic and Automation Incidents and Controversies", a non-partisan grassroots initiative for transparency, openness and accountability, a diverse set of individuals funded by individuals' donations, with no commercial funding (about page), and the developing organisation in the OECD's catalogue. It is independent of government and industry and read by researchers, academics, teachers, NGOs, journalists, policymakers and industry experts (OECD); its weekly Alert newsletter, read in 92 countries, is by Charlie Pownall in its Substack metadata.

It holds incidents, systems and datasets, entries numbered to AIAAIC2276 on 29 October 2026, classified by five taxonomies and carrying dates, locations, developers, technologies and harms searchable by attribute (repository page; EthicAI). An entry gives operator, developer, country, sector, purpose, technology and issue, links its sources and a Wikipedia gloss, and carries a page type, as the May 2024 entry on Google AI Overviews telling users to add glue to pizzas shows, typed "Issue"; AIAAIC2256 records Google's AI summaries giving cancer patients wrong advice.

Anyone may report an incident or improve a page (repository and entry pages), and EthicAI finds its submissions more open and its array wider than the OECD monitor's, the AIAAIC grassroots and the two complementary.

Its content is CC BY-SA 4.0 (its page; the OECD, free of charge, open source/permissive), and the catalogue calls the entry always up to date.

The OECD tags it an incident database and types it a risk-management, awareness and education tool, not vetted by the OECD; EthicAI defines the AI incident broadly and names the trackers' limits, underreporting, verification and coverage gaps, calling them under the radar but critical.

Its resources include an AI ethics glossary; Wikipedia redirects the title AIAAIC (since 15 September 2025) to a section of Ethics of artificial intelligence that the article does not have and that does not name it.

On its own page the AIAAIC Repository is "the independent, grassroots public interest collection of incidents and ethical controversies caused by and associated with AI, algorithms, and automation"; the OECD catalogue (8 June 2023) describes an independent, open public interest resource detailing incidents and controversies, its card reading "open-access", and EthicAI (24 April 2025) a collective memory documenting incidents where AI systems cause or contribute to harms, the repository's card listing its incidents as harms. It began in June 2019 as a private, professional project to understand the reputational risks of AI and became an open, public interest initiative (OECD); EthicAI calls it a private initiative of 2019, now open source. Its maker is AIAAIC, "AI, Algorithmic and Automation Incidents and Controversies", a non-partisan grassroots initiative for transparency, openness and accountability, a diverse set of individuals funded by individuals' donations, with no commercial funding (about page), and the developing organisation in the OECD's catalogue. It is independent of government and industry and read by researchers, academics, teachers, NGOs, journalists, policymakers and industry experts (OECD); its weekly Alert newsletter, read in 92 countries, is by Charlie Pownall in its Substack metadata. It holds incidents, systems and datasets, entries numbered to AIAAIC2276 on 29 October 2026, classified by five taxonomies and carrying dates, locations, developers, technologies and harms searchable by attribute (repository page; EthicAI). An entry gives operator, developer, country, sector, purpose, technology and issue, links its sources and a Wikipedia gloss, and carries a page type, as the May 2024 entry on Google AI Overviews telling users to add glue to pizzas shows, typed "Issue"; AIAAIC2256 records Google's AI summaries giving cancer patients wrong advice. Anyone may report an incident or improve a page (repository and entry pages), and EthicAI finds its submissions more open and its array wider than the OECD monitor's, the AIAAIC grassroots and the two complementary. Its content is CC BY-SA 4.0 (its page; the OECD, free of charge, open source/permissive), and the catalogue calls the entry always up to date. The OECD tags it an incident database and types it a risk-management, awareness and education tool, not vetted by the OECD; EthicAI defines the AI incident broadly and names the trackers' limits, underreporting, verification and coverage gaps, calling them under the radar but critical. Its resources include an AI ethics glossary; Wikipedia redirects the title AIAAIC (since 15 September 2025) to a section of Ethics of artificial intelligence that the article does not have and that does not name it.

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology1402 words

The AIAAIC Repository is a database of incidents and controversies driven by AI, algorithmic and automation systems (MMRS record), its unit the incident or controversy involving such a system (MMRS record), and on its own page "The independent, grassroots public interest collection of incidents and ethical controversies caused by and associated with AI, algorithms, and automation." The OECD's catalogue entry (uploaded 8 June 2023) describes "an independent, open, public interest resource" detailing incidents and controversies, its card on the Overview's rail reading "independent, open-access", the repository's own card lists its incidents as AI and algorithmic automation harms from autonomous vehicle crashes to generative AI copyright and training, and EthicAI (24 April 2025) gives its goal as "systematically documenting incidents where AI systems cause or contribute to harms", a collective memory for the AI field; the MMRS record quotes the catalogue's description and takes the repository's self-description from it. On the MMRS record's reading its unit is wider than harm: a controversy enters as a controversy, so public dispute about a system is recorded alongside events in which a system caused damage, admission does not require harm, and its name carries three kinds of system, algorithmic and automated as well as AI. It is kept by AIAAIC, which its about page expands as "AI, Algorithmic and Automation Incidents and Controversies" and calls "an independent, politically and technologically non-partisan grassroots public interest initiative" for AI, algorithmic and automation transparency, openness and accountability; the OECD catalogue names aiaaic as its developing organisation, and the MMRS record gives AIAAIC as operator from the repository's page, with the expansion as the repository's other name. Who runs it is, on the about page, "a diverse set of individuals across the world", funded by individuals' donations and taking no funding or in-kind donations from commercial entities; the page names no person, and the MMRS record lists who runs the repository as not yet checked. Its mission is "to make AI, algorithmic and automation systems transparent, open and accountable", by data for academic and civil society entities, by education and by making the case to policymakers and businesses, on the belief that everyone should know when such a system is used on them (about page). It started in June 2019 "as a private, professional project to better understand the reputational risks of artificial intelligence" and evolved into an open, public interest initiative that collects, dissects, examines and divulges incidents and issues (OECD catalogue, which the MMRS record quotes and dates it from); EthicAI writes that it was launched as a private initiative in 2019 and is now an open source, public interest initiative. It is independent of government and industry, and used by researchers, academics, teachers, NGOs (the catalogue writes "NGS"), journalists, policymakers and industry experts (OECD catalogue). It holds three collections, incidents, systems and datasets, its entries numbered in one series, the highest listed on 29 October 2026 AIAAIC2276, an upper bound on their count since the list skips numbers (repository page); EthicAI describes entries carrying incident dates, locations, system developers, technologies and harms, searchable and filterable by those attributes. One entry page, read for the per-entry fields the MMRS record left unchecked, gives operator, developer, country, sector, purpose, technology and issue ("Operator: Google users", "Developer: Google"), links its system page, the developer's own document and seven news, commentary and analysis sources by URL, glosses hallucination with Wikipedia's definition credited to Wikipedia, and closes with a page type ("Type: Issue") and its published and updated months. It classifies by five taxonomies, ethical issue, external harm, consequence, news trigger and response (repository page), which EthicAI describes as a taxonomy of incident types and causes that continues to evolve as more data is collected. Anyone may report an incident or controversy, from the repository page and from every entry ("Report incident 🔥 | Improve page 💁 | Access database 🔢"), and EthicAI sets its intake against the OECD monitor's: "AIAAIC allows more open submissions from a broader set of contributors", where AIM is curated with controlled input; the MMRS record lists intake, fields and count as not yet checked. Its content is under CC BY-SA 4.0 by its own page ("AIAAIC content is available to use, copy, adapt, and redistribute under a CC BY-SA 4.0 licence"), and the OECD catalogue gives its usage rights as open source/permissive, Creative Commons and free of charge and its licence as CC BY-SA 4.0 International, which the MMRS record takes from the catalogue. The catalogue's entries are their originating authors' and "are not vetted or endorsed by the OECD or its member countries", and the entry records the tool as a published document whose validity is "Always up to date". EthicAI names the limits of the incident trackers, underreporting, the verification of submitted incidents and coverage gaps, and finds them under the radar outside specialist circles and critical tools in the conversation on AI risk and accountability. The MMRS record states its own limits and keeps itself apart from the entity: its entry pages, intake process and current count were not read for it, its three sources were read on 2026-10-28 (the repository page for scope and projects, the catalogue for start, scope and licence, the newsletter's about page for its author), the lifecycle is active as observed that day, and each assertion carries a source and a basis. The OECD tags it "incident database" and types it a risk management framework, an awareness-building and an education and training tool, the MMRS record's kind is database, and EthicAI defines the AI incident such trackers hold as "any situation where an AI system causes, contributes to, or is associated with an outcome that negatively impacts individuals, groups, systems, or the environment". Against the OECD AI Incidents and Hazards Monitor, EthicAI finds "AIAAIC is grassroots and community-driven" where AIM has formal international backing, and its array wider, "from technical failures to social impacts", where AIM leans to policy-relevant cases, the two "complementary, not competitive". The MMRS record places it as the oldest of the census's three harm repositories, beside the AI Incident Database and the OECD monitor, its typed neighbours, its role harm; the AI Incident Database's record names it a neighbour in the harm basin, marks it by "AIAAIC, controversies, algorithmic and automation", and checks that the AIID is "not merged with the OECD monitor or AIAAIC". AIAAIC's weekly Alert newsletter details the latest incidents and controversies and developments in transparency and accountability and is read in 92 countries by its own account (its about page); the page body names no person, its Substack metadata reads "AIAAIC, by Charlie Pownall", and the MMRS record gives Pownall as the newsletter's writer and the repository as the newsletter's subject. The repository's resources include a list of AI and algorithmic repositories, registers and databases and an AI ethics glossary (repository page), and the archive's Hexagonal Lexical Engine (#543, 10 March 2026) names "AI Ethics glossaries (AIAAIC, AI Incident DB)" as the venue for definitions with citations of three of its terms, semantic liquidation, ghost governance and taxonomic violence. Google AI Overviews is among the systems it records, and a 2026 entry (AIAAIC2256) records Google's AI summaries giving cancer patients wrong advice (repository page); the entry of May 2024 records the Overviews telling users to add glue to pizzas, criticised for "factually inaccurate, misleading and nonsensical answers", the glue traced to a troll post and rocks recommended from a satirical Onion article, and Google saying it would refine them by limiting which queries generate summaries. Wikipedia has no article for it: the title AIAAIC redirects, since 15 September 2025, to a section "AI, Algorithmic, and Automation Incidents and Controversies" of Ethics of artificial intelligence, which the article as fetched on 29 October 2026 does not have, and the article names neither AIAAIC nor its expansion. The MMRS record carries the capture at the name as the composition layer's account of the entity, and the Capture Registry (2026-10-29) records that June 2019, 'a private initiative', CC BY-SA 4.0 and 'incidents and controversies' are the OECD catalogue's, where the record took them, a finding checked against the record and the entity's own pages; the catalogue's words are "a private, professional project", and "a private initiative" is EthicAI's. Composition and record were built from the same third-party catalogue and agree, neither names who runs the repository, and the composition names no person, not even the newsletter's writer the record names (Capture Registry, 2026-10-29).

Substituted reading: the start's purpose, in both cards 'to better understand the reputational risks of artificial intelligence' (F12, F21), is composed as 'to monitor transparency and accountability'; the nearest words in the field are the operator's mission ('transparent, open and accountable', F34, an own page T did not surface), the OECD's tag 'transparency' (F17) and EthicAI's 'fostering transparency' (outside the ledgered spans).
